econ-game-01-c3.text: Steven Kuhn (2025). Prisoner's Dilemma. Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy.
econ-game-01-c3.quote: whatever the other does, each is better off confessing than remaining silent
econ-game-01-c3.claim: If you're one of the suspects, defection is better regardless of what the other does.

econ-game-01-c3.text: Steven Kuhn (2025). Prisoner's Dilemma. Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy.
econ-game-01-c3.quote: (C,C) is strictly preferred by each to (D,D)
econ-game-01-c3.claim: Individual rationality leads to a collectively bad outcome.

econ-game-01-c4.text: Don Ross (2023). Game Theory. Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy.
econ-game-01-c4.quote: known as iterated elimination of strictly dominated strategies
econ-game-01-c4.claim: That gives a simple solution method called iterated elimination of dominated strategies.

econ-game-02-c2.text: (1994). Press release: The Prize in Economic Sciences 1994. NobelPrize.org.
econ-game-02-c2.quote: Moreover, Nash showed that for every game with a finite number of players, there exists an equilibrium in mixed strategies.
econ-game-02-c2.claim: John Nash's 1950 result: every finite game has at least one Nash equilibrium (possibly in mixed strategies).

econ-game-02-c4.text: Don Ross. Game Theory. Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy.
econ-game-02-c4.quote: There, it makes sense to eliminate the most attractive outcome, joint refusal to confess, because both players have incentives to unilaterally deviate from it, so it is not an NE.
econ-game-02-c4.claim: The cooperate-cooperate outcome in the prisoner's dilemma is Pareto efficient but not a Nash equilibrium.

econ-game-03-c1.text: (1994). Press release: The Prize in Economic Sciences 1994. NobelPrize.org.
econ-game-03-c1.quote: A mixed strategy is a probability distribution of a player’s available strategies, whereby a player is assumed to choose a certain “pure” strategy with some probability.
econ-game-03-c1.claim: Each player randomizes over their pure strategies according to some probability distribution.

econ-game-03-c4.text: (1994). Press release: The Prize in Economic Sciences 1994. NobelPrize.org.
econ-game-03-c4.quote: Moreover, Nash showed that for every game with a finite number of players, there exists an equilibrium in mixed strategies.
econ-game-03-c4.claim: Nash's existence theorem: every finite game has at least one Nash equilibrium in mixed strategies.

econ-game-04-c1.text: Steven Kuhn. Prisoner’s Dilemma. Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy.
econ-game-04-c1.quote: Tree diagrams like Figure 6 are said to be extensive-form game representations, whereas the payoff matrices given previously are normal-form representations.
econ-game-04-c1.claim: The extensive form represents this with a game tree.

econ-game-04-c2.text: Don Ross. Game Theory. Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy.
econ-game-04-c2.quote: Just imagine the player (or analyst) beginning at the end of the tree, where outcomes are displayed, and then working backwards from these, looking for sets of strategies that describe paths leading to them.
econ-game-04-c2.claim: Start at the end of the tree and work backward.

econ-game-04-c3.text: (1994). Press release: The Prize in Economic Sciences 1994. NobelPrize.org.
econ-game-04-c3.quote: In addition, however, it fulfills Selten’s requirement of subgame perfection, which thus implies systematic formalization of the requirement that only credible threats should be taken into account.
econ-game-04-c3.claim: Subgame perfection rules out non-credible threats.

econ-game-04-c3.text: (1994). Press release: The Prize in Economic Sciences 1994. NobelPrize.org.
econ-game-04-c3.quote: A potential competitor who realizes this will establish himself on the market and the monopolist, confronted with fait accompli, will not start a price war.
econ-game-04-c3.claim: Once the entrant has entered, the incumbent's best response is to accommodate, not fight.

econ-game-05-c1.text: (2005). Press release: The Prize in Economic Sciences 2005. NobelPrize.org.
econ-game-05-c1.quote: In many real-world situations, cooperation may be easier to sustain in a long-term relationship than in a single encounter.
econ-game-05-c1.claim: The shadow of the future creates incentives for cooperation that don't exist in one-shot play.

econ-game-05-c2.text: Steven Kuhn. Prisoner’s Dilemma. Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy.
econ-game-05-c2.quote: The strategy that scored highest in Axelrod’s initial tournament, Tit for Tat (henceforth TFT), simply cooperates on the first round and imitates its opponent’s previous move thereafter.
econ-game-05-c2.claim: Cooperate on the first move; then copy whatever the opponent did last time.

econ-game-05-c2.text: Steven Kuhn. Prisoner’s Dilemma. Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy.
econ-game-05-c2.quote: Axelrod attributed the success of TFT to four properties.
econ-game-05-c2.claim: These four properties together explain its success against a wide range of strategies.

econ-game-05-c3.text: Don Ross. Game Theory. Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy.
econ-game-05-c3.quote: Many other strategies, such as Grim (cooperate until defected against by a player, then defect against that defector unconditionally forever) and Tit-for-two-tats (cooperate until defected against twice by a player, then defect once before reverting to cooperation) occur in various NE combinations.
econ-game-05-c3.claim: Grim trigger: cooperate as long as the other does; once they defect, defect forever.

econ-game-06-c1.text: (1994). Press release: The Prize in Economic Sciences 1994. NobelPrize.org.
econ-game-06-c1.quote: Harsanyi postulated that every player is one of several “types”, where each type corresponds to a set of possible preferences for the player and a (subjective) probability distribution over the other players’ types.
econ-game-06-c1.claim: Each player has a type, drawn from some distribution, that summarizes their private information.

econ-game-06-c1.text: (1994). Press release: The Prize in Economic Sciences 1994. NobelPrize.org.
econ-game-06-c1.quote: In the jargon of game theory, he thereby transformed games with incomplete information into games with imperfect information.
econ-game-06-c1.claim: This converts incomplete-information games into well-defined games of imperfect information.

econ-game-06-c4.text: (2001). Press release: The Prize in Economic Sciences 2001. NobelPrize.org.
econ-game-06-c4.quote: George Akerlof demonstrated how a market where sellers have more information than buyers about product quality can contract into an adverse selection of low-quality products.
econ-game-06-c4.claim: George Akerlof's 1970 paper (Nobel 2001) shows how private information can collapse a market.

econ-game-06-c5.text: (2001). Press release: The Prize in Economic Sciences 2001. NobelPrize.org.
econ-game-06-c5.quote: Michael Spence identified an important form of adjustment by individual market participants, where the better informed take costly actions in an attempt to improve on their market outcome by credibly transmitting information to the poorly informed.
econ-game-06-c5.claim: Credible signaling requires the signal to be costly, and costlier for low types than high types.
